what_it_does: Every chip has a clock — a regular electrical pulse that keeps all its parts working in step, like a drummer keeping a band in time. 'Clock skew scheduling' means deliberately making the clock pulse arrive at different parts of the chip at slightly different times, so that the slowest operations get a head start and the chip can run faster overall. The bottleneck in computing the best skew schedule is extracting all the timing paths between the chip's storage elements (flip-flops — the tiny memory cells that hold data between clock pulses), which is extremely slow for large chips. This paper introduces an iterative algorithm that builds only the parts of that timing-path graph it actually needs, using a propagation technique that avoids constructing the full graph upfront. The result is claimed to be significantly faster while still finding good skew assignments, though quantitative speedup data requires the full paper.
